title: Leading KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit
web_title: 5. Leading KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit
book_title: Chapter 5: Management on Trial — Leading KPIs & Walking the Talk

epigraph.quote: “We remain committed to operational excellence, working capital optimization and executing projects timely.”
epigraph.author: M.M. Kabra, Managing Director, FY26 results press release, 5 May 2026

web_blocks.html: Profit is the last thing to move in a facade contractor. Six operating numbers move first: order book against billing, capacity and its use, operating margin by half-year, net working capital against revenue, customer concentration, and interest plus borrowings. The company reports only half-yearly, so each KPI in this chapter is a half-year or a dated disclosure. Revenue, margin, interest, profit, borrowings and cash flow can be read from the filings. Order book appears only in two press releases, capacity use only in a July 2026 filing, and customer concentration has not been published since the prospectus [2][5][26][27][28].

Net trade working capital as % of revenue
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue and margin rise. The three rows that cost money, interest, borrowings and working capital, rise faster, and the two rows that would show demand quality, order book and concentration, go silent.

web_blocks.html: Order book is the first KPI. Management gave about ₹302 Cr in May 2025 and about ₹300 Cr in May 2026 [27][2]. Revenue rose ₹29.3 Cr between the two dates, so orders won roughly equalled revenue billed, about ₹137 Cr (my arithmetic: revenue plus the change in book). A book-to-bill ratio near 1.0 and cover of 2.2 times FY26 revenue are healthy. They do not match a plan to grow 44% in FY27, because a flat book cannot support a step-up in billing. The H1 FY27 filing gave no order book at all [5].

Margin is the second. Operating margin excluding other income was 11.0% in FY25, 11.8% in FY26 and 13.5% in H1 FY27 on standalone figures (13.4% consolidated), against 12.4% in H1 FY26 (12.3% consolidated), an improvement of about 110 bps [1][5]. But H1 FY27 profit growth is not all operating. Other income was ₹2.0 Cr against ₹0.3 Cr a year earlier and explains 83% of the ₹2.1 Cr rise in pre-tax profit, while interest more than doubled to ₹2.25 Cr [5][26]. The third is working capital: net trade working capital (inventory plus receivables plus unbilled work less payables) went from about 41% of revenue at March 2024 to 55%, 64% and 66%. Since March 2024 each extra rupee of revenue has come with roughly one extra rupee of working capital (approximate, because the FY24 balance sheet does not split unbilled work) [4][1][5]. Customer advances fell from ₹9.5 Cr to ₹5.8 Cr in FY26 [1]. Concentration is a blind spot: the last list showed the top ten customers at 59% of revenue, with L&T entities at about 12% [3].

Two further KPIs are not reported at all: the facade-versus-window mix and the contribution of new lines. Segment reporting is single, and FY26 revenue was 98.9% windows and facade work and 1.1% tolling [1]. Management says 'the contribution of facades will increase gradually leading to better execution and margin profiles' [2], but without a split the claim cannot be tested. The subsidiary, Aluwind Clean-Tech, has booked no revenue and lost ₹0.09 Cr in H1 FY27, and the July 2026 solar-facade line carries an investment of 'depend on market scenario' [5][29][30]. Treat all three as options, not as drivers of FY27.

web_blocks.takeaway: The guidance needs more output than the plant was stated to hold, in a facade shop already full, from a book that has not grown. New capacity arrives only in Q1 FY28.

web_blocks.html: The runway is not the problem. Ken Research sees the combined market at ₹35,130 Cr growing 11.9% a year, so Aluwind at 0.4% share faces no demand ceiling [35]. The ceilings are the plant and the balance sheet. One caution on the capacity table: revenue per sq m is so stable across four periods (₹7,475 to ₹7,586) that the prospectus utilisation figures look derived from revenue at a fixed rate, not measured on the shop floor. That is my inference, and it means the 92% FY26 figure is an estimate. On capital, ₹60 Cr of extra revenue at 65% working capital needs about ₹39 Cr of new funding, while annual profit is about ₹11 Cr, so roughly ₹28 Cr would come from banks (my arithmetic). At the roughly one-to-one marginal rate seen between FY24 and FY26 the need would be about ₹60 Cr and bank funding about ₹49 Cr, which would take borrowings toward ₹95 Cr; the ₹60 Cr borrowing trigger in this report assumes the lower, 65% case. I put the chance of FY27 revenue reaching ₹200 Cr at 10% or less, and the likely range at ₹150 Cr to ₹170 Cr, about 70%.

Now the audit. The standard is simple: take what management or the prospectus said, find the next filing that tests it, and score it as delivered, partly, missed or too early. Management's own words matter more than my summary, so they are quoted where possible. The prospectus said the company would 'usually bill and collect on relatively short cycles' and planned 'a lower inventory holding period' [3]. The FY25 annual report promised 'facility modernization and capacity enhancement' and said the company would 'explore export markets' [25]. The May 2026 press release said it was 'confident of achieving its guided turnover target of ₹200 crore for FY27, driven by improved execution and margin expansion' [2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Management does what it can control, such as spending the IPO money as promised and buying machines. It misses on what depends on customers and suppliers, which is where cash is made.

web_blocks.html: Test the epigraph against the cash flow statement. The quote was given in May 2026, so the FY26 statement is the baseline and H1 FY27 is the first test. FY26 operating cash flow was -₹16.3 Cr, inventory absorbed ₹27.0 Cr and working capital as a whole ₹30.0 Cr [1]. In H1 FY27 operating cash flow turned to +₹0.8 Cr: inventory released ₹6.2 Cr, but receivables rose ₹10.3 Cr and payables fell ₹3.5 Cr [5]. That is one improvement and two reversals, so I score the quote 'partly, too early'. My independent view is that management is candid in its filings, which print retention and ageing tables, but its public message stresses revenue and order book while the cash flow statement carries the harder news. The CFO, company secretary and an independent director all changed between May and September 2026 [1][29][31]. That is not proof of trouble, but it is not the continuity the quote promises.

book_paragraphs: Imagine you are standing in the finance office of a facade contractor on the day the half-year closes. You could read the profit line. I would rather you looked at six numbers that move before profit does. How big is the order book compared with billing? How full is the plant? What margin does each half-year earn? How much cash is tied up in unfinished work for each rupee of revenue? How concentrated are the customers? And what is the interest bill doing? Aluwind reports only twice a year, so these are half-year readings, and some are not disclosed at all. Revenue, margin, interest, profit, borrowings and cash flow come from the filings. The order book appears in just two press releases, capacity use in one July 2026 filing, and the customer list has not been published since the March 2024 prospectus [2][3][5][26][27][28].

Start with orders, because they are what the plant will build. Management said the order book was about ₹302 Cr in May 2025 and about ₹300 Cr in May 2026 [27][2]. In between, revenue rose by ₹29.3 Cr. If you add revenue to the change in the book, you get orders won of about ₹137 Cr, which is almost the same as revenue billed. So the company is winning about as much as it builds, a ratio near 1.0, and holds 2.2 years of work. That is a healthy base. But it is the wrong shape for a company that says it will grow 44% next year. A flat order book cannot feed a jump in billing. The half-year filing of November 2026 gave no order book at all [5].

Margin comes next. Strip out other income, and operating margin was 11.0% in FY25 and 11.8% in FY26. In H1 FY27 it was 13.5% against 12.4% a year earlier on standalone figures (13.4% and 12.3% consolidated), about 110 bps better [1][5]. That is real progress, and I want to give it credit. Then look beneath the profit line. Other income was ₹2.0 Cr in H1 FY27 against ₹0.3 Cr a year before, and that jump explains 83% of the rise in pre-tax profit. Interest more than doubled to ₹2.25 Cr [5][26]. So the improvement at the operating level was partly consumed by the cost of the debt that funds the work, and partly replaced by income that is not from fabrication.

Now the number I care most about. Add inventory, receivables and unbilled work, and subtract what the company owes suppliers. That net trade working capital was about 41% of revenue at March 2024, 55% at March 2025, 64% at March 2026 and 66% at September 2026. Since March 2024, each extra rupee of revenue has needed about one extra rupee of working capital. That figure is approximate, since the FY24 balance sheet does not split unbilled work [4][1][5]. Customers also paid less up front: advances fell from ₹9.5 Cr to ₹5.8 Cr in FY26 [1]. Think of a restaurant that must buy the ingredients for the next ten tables before the last ten have paid. Growth makes that restaurant hungrier for cash, not richer.

Two more numbers are simply missing. The company does not split facade from window revenue, and it reports a single segment. In FY26, 98.9% of revenue was windows and facade work and 1.1% was tolling [1]. Management says 'the contribution of facades will increase gradually leading to better execution and margin profiles' [2]. Without a split, you cannot check that. The cleaning subsidiary has no revenue yet and lost ₹0.09 Cr in H1 FY27, and the new solar-facade line has an investment amount of 'depend on market scenario' [5][29][30]. I treat all of these as options, not as drivers of FY27.

How much can the plant build? The prospectus put installed capacity at 200,224 square metres a year [3]. Divide the revenue of each earlier period by the output it reported and you get about ₹7,500 per square metre every time, from ₹7,475 to ₹7,586. That is suspiciously steady, and it makes me think the utilisation figures were derived from revenue, not measured on the floor. Use the ₹7,500 anyway. FY26 revenue then needs about 1.85 lakh square metres, or 92% of the prospectus capacity. The ₹200 Cr guidance needs about 2.67 lakh, or 133% of the capacity stated at the March 2024 prospectus and about 102% of the roughly 2.6 lakh square metres rated since the June 2025 CNC addition (Chapter 3). In July 2026 the company said its facade shop makes up to 20 panels a day and is 'close to full utilization'. It approved a ₹20 Cr line for 50 panels a day, bank funded, ready from Q1 of FY2027-28 [28]. To reach ₹200 Cr, H2 FY27 must bill ₹126.0 Cr, 72% more than H2 FY26's ₹73.1 Cr, and 67% of the ₹300 Cr order book must convert within a year.

The market is not the limit. Ken Research sees a ₹35,130 Cr market growing near 11.9% a year, and Aluwind holds about 0.4% [35]. The limits are the shed and the balance sheet. Each ₹60 Cr of extra revenue at 65% working capital needs about ₹39 Cr of funding, while a year of profit is about ₹11 Cr. About ₹28 Cr would come from banks, or about ₹49 Cr if working capital keeps absorbing a rupee for every extra rupee of sales, as it did from FY24 to FY26. Those are my calculations, not company figures. I give FY27 revenue of ₹200 Cr a chance of 10% or less. My likely range is ₹150 Cr to ₹170 Cr, with about 70% confidence.

Now to the part you may find most useful: did management do what it said? I gave myself a simple rule. Take the promise, find the next filing that tests it, and score it delivered, partly, missed or too early. First, the IPO money. The prospectus asked for ₹20.45 Cr for working capital and ₹6.50 Cr for general purposes. The company used ₹20.45 Cr, ₹6.55 Cr and ₹2.70 Cr of issue costs, all by 30 September 2025, and an auditor's certificate of November 2025 reports no deviation [1][26]. Delivered.

Second, the working capital plan. In the prospectus the company said it would 'usually bill and collect on relatively short cycles', and planned for FY26 an inventory of ₹21.5 Cr, payables of ₹8.7 Cr and short-term borrowings of just ₹7.8 Cr [3]. At March 2026 inventory was ₹57.6 Cr, about 207 days of materials consumed (167 on the company's own ratio basis), payables ₹40.1 Cr and borrowings ₹41.3 Cr. Only receivable days beat the plan, at 103 against 114 [1]. That is a miss, and not a small one. Inventory was 2.7 times the plan, and the company leaned on suppliers and banks for the difference.

Third, modernisation and expansion. The prospectus said the plant 'operates on semi automation' and the company would modernise. The FY25 report promised 'facility modernization and capacity enhancement' [3][25]. The company bought a 5-axis CNC machine and an automated powder-coating line, spent ₹4.5 Cr on assets in FY26 and took a ₹2.45 Cr machinery loan [1][27]. It named Chennai and Madurai projects, but not revenue from Karnataka, Gujarat or Telangana [2]. Partly delivered. Fourth, the FY27 target. The press release said the company was 'confident of achieving its guided turnover target of ₹200 crore for FY27, driven by improved execution and margin expansion' [2]. Margin has improved about 110 bps and revenue is up 13% in H1, but the plant and book arithmetic above is against it. Too early, and stretched.

Fifth, exports and partnerships. The FY25 report spoke of exploring exports and building partnerships to raise capacity use [25]. The tolling contract with Hindalco added ₹1.57 Cr in FY26, 1.1% of revenue, and foreign exchange earned was nil in both years [1]. On 5 November 2026 the company hired Ajay Porwal as President, Global Business 'to explore the possibility of expanding its business activities into the export market' [5]. Tolling delivered, exports too early.

Finally, the sentence at the top of this chapter. The Managing Director said, 'We remain committed to operational excellence, working capital optimization and executing projects timely' [2]. Hold it against the cash flow statement. FY26 operating cash flow was -₹16.3 Cr, inventory absorbed ₹27.0 Cr and working capital as a whole ₹30.0 Cr [1]. H1 FY27 turned to +₹0.8 Cr: inventory released ₹6.2 Cr, but receivables rose ₹10.3 Cr and payables fell ₹3.5 Cr [5]. One improvement, two reversals. My score is partly, and too early to say more. The CFO, the company secretary and an independent director all changed between May and September 2026 [1][29][31]. I would not read that as trouble. I would read it as a company whose finance team is new just when the working capital questions get hard.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Management keeps the promises it can keep alone: it spent the IPO money as stated and bought machines. It misses the ones that need customers and suppliers to cooperate, and those are the promises that make cash. Trust the next filings, not the guidance: operating cash flow above profit for two halves in a row would tell you more than another order book headline.
